extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotelian ethics; scholars of moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_short: interpreting Aristotle on pleasure and happiness
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Aristotle's evaluative claims about Friendship, Pleasure, and Happiness from Book X of the Nicomachean Ethics. Focuses on what counts as good/choice-worthy actions, kinds of pleasure, and the nature of the happy life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity toward those in need
rubrics_metrics.description: One should show liberality toward those who are in need and who do not demand it as a right; doing so is creditable and pleasant to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give willingly to friends in need (when they do not claim it as a right); avoid appearing sulky when declining sympathy or help. Example/nuance: occasional caution against appearing sullenness is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharing good fortune with friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends should readily share in one another’s good fortune and be willing to forward it in any way they can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act to help friends in their successes because friends need one another for this; but be moderate in eagerness to receive advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is choice-worthy and grounded in intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence and intimacy of friends is choice-worthy; friends most value intimacy and choose it above other goods because Friendship is communion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intimacy is expressed by shared activities (drinking, hunting, study, gymnastic exercises); friendships are enacted by participating in what each most likes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good friendships improve partners; bad friendships corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: The Friendship of the good grows and improves partners by mutual correction; the Friendship of the wicked is depraved because they share in badness and make one another worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good friends receive beneficial impressions from one another; expect moral improvement through repeated intercourse. Anti-pattern: friendships that reinforce vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as an object of choice (Eudoxus' claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eudoxus argued Pleasure is the Chief Good because all (rational and irrational) aim at it; Pleasure is chosen for its own sake and opposed to Pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments noted: universality of aiming at pleasure (analogy to nourishment), choice for itself, and that Pleasure increases the worth of other goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good cannot be merely Pleasure (Plato's counterargument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Against Pleasure-as-Chief-Good: when combined with Practical Wisdom the pleasurable life is more choice-worthy, so simple Pleasure cannot be the Chief Good since the Chief Good cannot be improved by addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinction between simple and compound goods; Plato's reasoning: if a compound is better than simple Pleasure, simple Pleasure is not the supreme end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures differ in kind (higher vs base pleasures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures are not homogeneous: some are unmixed and higher (e.g., intellectual pleasures, mathematical studies), others are base or disgraceful and not truly pleasant except to depraved tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pleasures by their sources (intellectual vs bodily). Examples: pleasures of smell/sense vs pleasures of mathematical study. Anti-pattern: treating all pleasures as equally good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is a 'whole', not a Movement or Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is complete at any moment and is not a Movement or Generation (unlike walking or building), because it lacks the temporal incompleteness characteristic of movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare pleasure to an act of Sight which is whole at an instant; reject accounts that treat Pleasure as merely a process or supply after lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure accompanies the perfect working of a percipient faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Every percipient faculty in its best state working upon the best object produces the most perfect and most pleasant pleasure; pleasure attends intellectual and sensory operation when they are excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure perfects an act of working as a supervening finish (like bloom at prime). Thus best pleasures are those arising from highest faculties acting upon best objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure perfects and increases the activity it accompanies
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper pleasure augments and refines the working it attends (e.g., pleasure in geometry promotes careful geometric work); pleasure makes work more enduring and better of its kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive feedback: pleasure in an activity improves skill and diligence. Guidance: cultivate pleasures proper to virtuous or intellectual work to improve practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign pleasures hinder the activity at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures foreign to the activity undermine or destroy the current working (e.g., flute music distracting from discourse); the more pleasant foreign activity will push out the less pleasant one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: indulging pleasures unrelated to your current task. Practical implication: align pleasures with the activity you wish to sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures and pains are closely tied to the nature of the working
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures proper to a working differ from pains proper to it; pleasures proper to good workings are good, and those proper to bad workings are bad—desires for noble things praiseworthy, for base things blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pleasures relative to the moral quality of the activity they attend; recognize that pleasures may be indivisible from their workings, raising questions of identity between work and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures differ by species and by organism
rubrics_metrics.description: Each animal (including humans) has pleasures proper to its own works; what is pleasant to one species or person may be unpleasant to another (e.g., an ass prefers hay to gold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize pleasures across different natures; account for variations in constitution, health, and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: The good man's judgment as the measure of true pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that impress the good man as pleasant are the real pleasures; the good man's perception serves as measure because of his soundness and lack of corruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the responses of the virtuous as a normative guide to which pleasures are genuinely choice-worthy; caveat: depraved tastes misidentify pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is a working in accordance with excellence (not mere state)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is not a mere passive state (which could belong to someone vegetating) but a form of activity—a working in accordance with excellence—that is self-sufficient and an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank happiness among actions chosen for their own sake; emphasize activities expressing excellence (virtues) rather than mere states or amusements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amusement and rest are not the final End
rubrics_metrics.description: Amusement and bodily pleasures are not the End (Happiness); rest is adopted with a view to further working and amusement is an appurtenance of Happiness but not its substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish appurtenances (leisure pursuits) from constitutive elements of the happy life. Anti-pattern: treating lifelong amusement as the ultimate aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: The contemplative (intellectual) life is the highest form of Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of contemplation (activity of the intellect) is the perfect form of Happiness because it is highest in kind, most continuous, self-sufficient, pleasurable, and restful; it aims at no end beyond itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons offered: intellect is the highest internal principle; contemplation is continuous and can be exercised alone; contains pure and enduring pleasures; best approximates divine life. Practical implication: prioritize intellectual cultivation for highest happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/moral virtues yield second-best Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A life in accordance with moral excellence and Practical Wisdom is second in degree to the contemplative life; practical virtues are bound to the composite nature, passions, and social action and therefore less self-sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the importance of moral virtues and their unity with Practical Wisdom, but note their dependence on social conditions and passions; they are proper to human life though subordinate to contemplative activity.
